0.0.n: Sets the time for the pizza offer.

0.1.n: Marks 今日 as the topic of the sentence.

0.2.n: Gives the price exactly; the Japanese does not include a word meaning approximately.

0.3.n: Marks the price at which you can eat pizza.

0.5.n: A hesitation filler here, not the word used to point out something distant.

0.7.n: A food word borrowed from English.

0.8.m: pizza is what you can eat
0.8.n: Marks ピザ as the thing available to eat with the ability form 食べれる.

0.9.n: Casual ability form of 食べる; standard 食べられる includes ら.

0.10.n: The preceding phrase describes what kind of day it is.

0.11.n: Links the noun 日 to explanatory んです.

0.12.n: Short for の, adding an explanatory tone with です.

0.13.n: Makes the explanation polite as part of なんです.

0.14.n: Softly connects this background information to what follows, without necessarily expressing a strong contrast.

1.0.n: A first attempt at saying the event name, followed by a restart.

1.2.n: The name of the March 14 celebration of the mathematical constant pi.

1.3.n: Casual quotation marker used with いう to introduce a name.

1.4.n: With って, names the day mentioned in the previous line.

2.0.n: Casually emphasizes the number of people here, rather than describing them as remarkable individuals.

2.1.n: Japanese nouns do not require a plural ending; the context indicates many people.

2.2.n: Marks 人 as the subject of 並んでます.

2.3.n: Shortened polite form of 並んでいます, describing people currently waiting in line.

3.0.n: Signals that the speaker is making an estimate rather than stating something certain.

3.1.n: 時間 counts hours of duration, not a clock time.

3.2.n: Added after 1時間 to make a duration of ninety minutes.

3.3.n: Includes the stated amount, so 1時間半以上 means ninety minutes or more.

3.4.n: Negative form of 並ぶ; followed by と, it introduces the condition of not waiting.

3.5.n: After 並ばない, creates an unless condition: without waiting, the pizza will not be available at that price.

3.8.n: Marks the price paid for the pizza.

3.9.n: The food the speaker hopes to get at the discounted price.

3.10.n: Makes ピザ the topic within the statement about being unable to eat it.

3.11.n: Negative of casual 食べれる; the standard form is 食べられない.

3.12.n: Short for explanatory の, introducing the speaker’s tentative conclusion with じゃないかな.

3.13.n: Contraction of では; combines with ない in the tentative ending んじゃないかな.

3.14.n: Part of じゃないかな, which softens the conclusion rather than simply reversing the earlier negative.

3.15.n: Adds a questioning tone within かな, making the thought tentative.

3.16.n: With か, expresses the speaker’s uncertainty or private reflection.

3.17.n: Marks the preceding thought as the content of 思います.

3.18.n: Polite form of 思う, presenting the statement as the speaker’s opinion.

0.lit: Today, for 300 yen, um, pizza can be eaten—a day it is, you see, but…
0.tip: 食べれる is a common casual version of 食べられる, meaning can eat.

1.tip: っていう is a casual way to introduce what something is called.

2.lit: So many people are lining up.
2.tip: すごい人 here means a huge number of people, not amazing people.

3.lit: Probably, unless waiting at least one-and-a-half hours, pizza for three dollars cannot be eaten, I suppose, I think.
3.tip: A negative verb followed by と means unless: 並ばないと means unless you wait in line.
